# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–38 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 8)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer). Emperor of China dinner scheduled Monday, 8th July; election for Westminster borough Tuesday, 9th July. Chapters 37–38 set in Harrowgate hill farms and coastal towns; transitions to London.
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, Staveton, Bryngate, Beccles, Caversham, Pickering, Dunwick, Miremere, Dunholt, Gulton, Yarlton, Coldcombe).

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. Chapter 37: Expressed wonder at Alf (editor of "Evening Pulpit"), noting he has sailed "within the wind" but now risks three or four thousand pounds in legal expenses.

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. **Chapter 38: Elopement plan finalized with Marie. To depart Wednesday afternoon (5 P.M. train to Liverpool, arriving 10:15 P.M.; hotel at railway station). Marie and Didon to leave Thursday at 7 A.M. in separate cab with Marie's heavy baggage containing wedding dresses and jewels; Felix to board S.S. "Adriatic" Thursday morning without acknowledging them until at sea. Didon holds tickets under names "Madame and Mademoiselle Racine"; Felix to obtain his own ticket tomorrow. Financial arrangement: Didon to present Marie's father's cheque (payable to House or Bearer, signed Melmotte) to bank, obtain £250, deliver to Felix at club Monday 4 P.M. Felix determined not to proceed unless Didon brings full sum; hopes accident will occur permitting him to recede. Suspicious cheque may be missed, payment stopped, or Didon apprehended/absconding with funds. Will tell mother of plan if Didon delivers money (mother recommended elopement; may contribute additional funds). When Ruby demanded marriage, refused: "Marry, Ruby! No, I don't ever mean to marry." At Music Hall Tuesday (final night before departure), promised to say parting word to Ruby. Uncomfortable about enterprise; almost repents but lacks courage to recede. Prefers money in own pocket; fears bank might arrest him for stealing Melmotte's funds.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 36: Paul visited her at Welbeck Street; she told mother loves someone else and praises Roger as "rock of strength."

## Ruby Ruggles and Suitors

**Ruby Ruggles**: Granddaughter of Daniel Ruggles (Sheep's Acre). Pretty with long glossy ringlets. Working as servant/maid to Mrs. Pipkin (her aunt) at Islington. **Chapter 38: Danced with Felix at City Road Music-Hall. Fled grandfather Daniel Ruggles' house after he pulled her by hair when undressed. When Felix refused marriage demand, Roger Carbury warned her forcefully against Felix; praised John Crumb's nobility; extracted promise she would not see Felix again. Roger spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about Ruby's late hours. Ran away from Felix after dance in great dudgeon; with morning reflection, misery stronger than wrath. Without prospect of Felix, daily toil unbearable. Reconsidered: perhaps gentleman wouldn't like marriage proposal; maybe would speak if given another chance. Wrote Felix letter underscoring loves and regrets, asking if he'd be at Music Hall Saturday. Felix replied tersely: Tuesday (his final night before New York departure). Sought to attend Tuesday dance; Mrs. Pipkin refused, threatened to keep her in streets all night. Ruby initially crushed—lover would be there, appointment broken—but then pleaded: "Aunt Pipkin, let me go just this once."**

**John Crumb**: Country lover from Suffolk, "Bungay mealman." Chapter 35: After supper, moved to take Ruby's hand; Ruby fled. Rode to Carbury Hall searching for her. Chapter 37: Visited Roger at Carbury Manor. Expressed anguish about Felix "pulling of her about"; declared willingness to "swing for it" if Felix seduced her. Roger assured him Ruby was good girl and promised further supervision by Mrs. Pipkin. Resolved to send Mrs. Pipkin price of new blue cloak via Mixet's letter and money order.

**Daniel Ruggles**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm. Violent under gin and water; pulled Ruby by hair when undressed (witnessed by Sally Hockett). Told Roger "whoever it is ought to speak out his mind."

**Mrs. Pipkin**: Ruby's aunt at Islington; lets lodgings with five children. **Chapter 38: Feared Ruby would rattle at front door or climb over area gate; resolved to surrender neither key in her pocket, though feared she might collapse into tears if Ruby violent. Plans to ask Mrs. Hurtle to speak to Ruby, whom she'd listen to when wouldn't mind Mrs. Pipkin.**

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Crisis with Mrs. Hurtle (Chapter 37)**: At Lowestoft evening, Paul finally told Mrs. Hurtle he cannot join his lot with her—chiefly because his heart is elsewhere and because her antecedents have caused friends to warn him. Mrs. Hurtle responded with fury. Confessed she shot a man in Oregon (brought him down dead); saved herself. Insisted she is not disgraced; divorced from Caradoc Hurtle (drunkard, scoundrel) under Kansas law on grounds of cruelty and drunkenness; he made no appearance; Court granted it; made her property again her own. Questioned why condemned for protecting herself, saving her life from reprobate husband. Paul thought her words may have been necessary, especially in Oregon. Called him coward, said he trembles between her and Roger (his master). Called him mean wretch; declared she had shot another man ten minutes prior had she a weapon. Demanded acknowledgment of treachery; declared she would not stay but return Monday; would think and resolve what to do; would not bear this without seeking means of punishing him. Expected him Monday. Said if he was afraid to come, she would come to him and tell her story. Paul said he would wait upon her on return to town but would not fix day now; promised to write.

**Mrs. Hurtle's Aftermath (Chapter 37–38)**: After Paul departed, fell on knees, gave way to flood of tears, lay rolling on floor. Questioned: Should she never know rest? In almost all she said, spoke truth, though not all. Endured violence, been violent. Regarding money: honest. Regarding heart: loving. With heart of hearts loved this young Englishman. After all scheming, daring, charms, this end. She had run over on what seemed vain chance after receiving his letter. In marrying her he must give up all old allies, old haunts. Whole world changed to him. She knew Englishwomen would avoid her when past known. Scorned and feared in eastern cities, name a proverb for violence in far West—could not hope lot changed. She had reminded Paul she required asking often before consenting to be wife; hesitation arose from her own conviction of unfitness. Circumstances made her what she was; cruel circumstances; could not alter them now. Gradually believed in his love, lost herself in love for him, told herself she would change. Almost known it could not be so. **Chapter 38: Returned from Lowestoft on Monday; made trivial excuse to Mrs. Pipkin in mildest voice (place windy, too cold, disliked hotel). Mrs. Pipkin glad to see her back. Has not sent letter to Paul kept in pocket-book but still keeps it, at moments thinking she would send it, at others told herself never surrender last hope till every stone turned. It might still be possible to shame him into marriage. Promised Mrs. Pipkin she would speak to Ruby, though when making promise could not but think of her unfitness for task. Knew nothing of country; not single friend in it but Paul; had run after him with as little discretion as Ruby showing in running after her lover. Who was she to give advice to any female?**

**Paul's Return (Chapter 38)**: Roger expressed satisfaction at Paul's account, recalling pledge given as to return. "Let her follow you, and bear it," Roger said. "Of course you must suffer the effects of your own imprudence." Paul Montague returned to London by mail train that evening, sure he would thus avoid meeting with Mrs. Hurtle in railway-carriage.

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman, South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. **Chapter 37–38: Extremely busy with electioneering speeches, Committee members, dinner orders, commercial affairs. Told Felix only entitled to shares for £600 now, will see it put right. Proposed Paul Mexican embassy; tone dubious to Paul. Expressed relief dinner would be over, noting easier to make treaty with Emperor than give him dinner. Received Board meeting call; ran off to meeting connected with interior of Africa at Cannon Street Hotel.**

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well; forming own opinions. **Chapter 38: Elopement plan with Felix confirmed: Travel to Liverpool Thursday, board S.S. "Adriatic" at noon bound for New York. Marry on board or at New York. Return within month to force father's acceptance. Didon to pose as aunt; Felix as "Smith"; Marie as French girl. Had key to Grosvenor Square gardens; Didon to unlock gate. Obtained £200; awaits Felix's recovery of more funds. Secured wedding dresses from Madame Craik at shop in Mount Street (not yet arrived but will proceed whether they come or not). Will have all jewels; to go off in cab retrieved from behind house into mews. Plans not to go to bed night before, departure 7 A.M. in second cab with Didon. Robert (the man) to start earlier with heavy box. Nobody ever up before near nine; expects no interruption. Lord Nidderdale never kissed her despite engagement; he broke engagement; she never behaved bad to him.**

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no London expenses. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham. Dolly refused consent unless half produce given to him.

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has rooms in Bruton Street. **Chapter 37–38: Arrangement made: £5,000 pay off all tradesmen's debts, leave him comfortably possessed; other £20,000 make his property free. Went to Caversham, made own terms; father unable to move him. Returned early morning demanding cheque on Melmotte's bank payable to his own. Has not yet received single ten-pound note from sale. Threatens to employ Mr. Squercum (lawyer) if money not paid quickly.**

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made protest against Melmottes. Following morning received invitation to stay with them. By Sunday, present at Grosvenor Square.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. **Chapter 37–38: Visited Ruby at Islington; warned her forcefully against Felix; praised John Crumb's nobility; extracted promise she would not see Felix again. Spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about Ruby's late hours. Encountered Paul and Mrs. Hurtle at Lowestoft; greeted them coldly; reproved Paul severely regarding his conduct with Mrs. Hurtle. Counselled Paul marriage with her would be destruction; advised him to tell her mind and leave her. Upon Paul's return, expressed satisfaction, recalling pledge as to return: "Let her follow you, and bear it. Of course you must suffer the effects of your own imprudence."**

## Minor Characters
**Lord Alfred Grendall**: Nearly overwhelmed by electioneering; declared willingness to help Melmotte but nearly in rebellion. Burdened with seating arrangements for dinner.

**Miles Grendall**: Secretary to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour.

**Didon**: Marie's attendant; facilitates elopement plan; holds tickets under name "Madame Racine"; to receive £50 before boarding ship; to present Melmotte's cheque to bank and deliver £250 to Felix at club Monday 4 P.M.

**Father John Barham**: Priest, Beccles.

**Sally Hockett**: Witnessed Daniel Ruggles pulling Ruby by hair.

**Mr. Squercum**: Lawyer threatened employment by Dolly.

**Provincial Figures (Chapters 37–38)**: Orvie Hollett, Halan Hollett, Eldette, Jozek Hollett, Aewyn, Seena, Rozek, Ridette, Jotho Corrett, Ilrine Corrett, Wewyn Corrett (child), Colan Lindson, Manelle Corrett, Brenelle Brackwood, Thivie Brackwood, Votho Brackwood, Feten Lindner, Thiena Hollwood, Maric Lindson, Nelde, Nynelle Stenworth (husband pressed pewter comb into her hands, took nothing for it), Elnelle Lindson, Cotho (discussed salt prices), Gamira, Ilrald Hollwood (took Rorine Lindson in marriage at Coldcombe before autumn out; couple lived in Coldcombe from then on).
